enrichment.short_title: Category B pension backdating and claim requirement

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mrs Nelligan received a Category A retirement pension from 1986 and became entitled to a larger Category B pension when her husband reached 65 in 1992, but did not claim Category B until March 2000.
A Social Security Commissioner held that section 43(5) of the 1992 Benefits Act allowed backdating to 1992 because the Category B pension was the most favourable whether claimed or not.

The Secretary of State appealed, arguing section 1(1) of the 1992 Administration Act requires a claim before entitlement arises and section 43(5) only chooses between pensions already claimed or deemed claimed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission of the Social Security Commissioner against a decision allowing a Category B pension backdated to 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Mrs Nelligan was not entitled to Category B retirement pension before 2 December 1999.
enrichment.ratio: Section 43(5) of the 1992 Benefits Act is a mechanism for choosing between pensions to which entitlement has already been established, including by a claim or deemed claim under section 1 of the 1992 Administration Act; it does not override the general rule that benefit entitlement ordinarily depends on a timely claim.
legal_issues: Whether section 43(5) displaces the claim requirement in section 1(1) of the 1992 Administration Act
Interaction of Category A and Category B retirement pensions
Effect of regulation 9 and Schedule 1 of the 1987 Regulations on deemed claims
Legislative history following Insurance Officer v McCaffrey
index_terms: Secretary of State for Work and Pensions

confidence.notes: Full appellate reasoning on statutory interaction; outcome and principle clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Harassment injunction against animal rights protesters
key_facts: Huntingdon Life Sciences and its managing director sought an interim injunction against SHAC and associated protesters ahead of a planned World Day for Lab Animals demonstration.
The claimants alleged a sustained campaign of harassment including home visits, property damage, threats and targeting of suppliers and employees.
The court held the Act could not protect companies from harassment but could protect individual employees; a representative claim under CPR Part 19 was permitted for employees.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interim application on notice for injunctive relief under section 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, following an adjourned ex parte application.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction granted in amended terms for individual claimants against named defendants; corporate claimants could not sue under the Act.
enrichment.ratio: Although a limited company cannot be the victim of harassment under the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, targeted harassment of identifiable employees at home and work falls within the Act's stalking-like purpose; exclusion zones and representative proceedings may be appropriate where an arguable unlawful campaign is shown.
legal_issues: Whether the Protection from Harassment Act 1997 applies to companies
Whether mass protest activity is covered by the Act
Representative proceedings against unidentifiable protesters
Lawfulness and breadth of exclusion zones in protest injunctions

confidence.notes: Interim judgment with clear holdings on statutory scope and procedural issues; some cited first-instance reports lack neutral citations.

enrichment.short_title: Handling conspiracy appeal and confiscation sequencing
key_facts: Ruddick was convicted after a second trial of conspiracy to handle stolen vehicle parts following an aborted first trial caused by jury nobbling, for which he received three years' imprisonment.
He appealed on grounds relating to prejudicial evidence, jury directions, failure to call a witness and admission of red diesel evidence from the first trial.
On sentence he challenged confiscation procedure, the sequencing of costs and confiscation orders, and the totality of consecutive sentences totalling seven and a half years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction and sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division), with some grounds treated as applications for leave.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence reduced to five and a half years in total by substituting one and a half years for the three-and-a-half-year conspiracy sentence.
enrichment.ratio: Procedural requirements under section 72A of the 1988 Act are directory rather than invariably mandatory; a breach does not automatically render later confiscation or costs orders null, but the Court of Appeal may adjust financial orders under section 11(3) where justice requires.
legal_issues: Whether the conviction was unsafe due to prejudicial or misdirected evidence
Prosecution duty to call a defence-helpful witness
Validity of confiscation proceedings postponed without a fixed return date
Whether costs orders made before confiscation must be quashed
Totality of consecutive sentences including benefit fraud

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate judgment on both conviction safety and post-Sekhon confiscation procedure.

enrichment.short_title: Miscarriage of justice compensation assessment review
key_facts: Michael Hickey, Vincent Hickey and Michael O'Brien sought judicial review of compensation assessments by Lord Brennan QC under section 133 after their murder convictions were quashed.
The independent assessor had awarded substantial pecuniary and non-pecuniary sums but declined detailed breakdowns of general damages and deducted saved living expenses from loss of earnings.
Maurice Kay J held the assessor must apply analogous common law damages principles, including transparency after Thompson, and quashed saved living expenses deductions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of statutory miscarriage of justice compensation assessments by the independent assessor, heard together for three claimants.
enrichment.outcome: Mixed result: claims succeeded on breakdown of non-pecuniary loss and saved living expenses; failed on criminal record deductions, interest methodology, financial advice and mother's counselling costs.
enrichment.ratio: An assessor under section 133 must apply principles analogous to civil damages law where clear and analogous, including the transparency requirement from Thompson v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis; saved living expenses are not deductible from loss of earnings by analogy with Dews v National Coal Board.
legal_issues: Meaning of analogous civil damages principles in the Secretary of State's guidance note
Whether non-pecuniary compensation must be itemised
Approach to aggravated features and loss of liberty quantification
Deduction for saved living expenses during imprisonment
Deduction under section 133(4A)(c) for other convictions
Interest calculation for long-tail pecuniary losses

linked_authorities.name: Thompson v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis
English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd

confidence.notes: Long administrative judgment with detailed holdings on multiple assessment grounds; relief on costs deferred.

enrichment.short_title: Nearest relative provisions incompatible with Article 8
key_facts: M, a detained psychiatric patient, alleged childhood sexual abuse by her adoptive father who was automatically her nearest relative under the Mental Health Act 1983.
She could not apply to replace him as nearest relative, giving him access to information and statutory powers over her detention and discharge.
The Secretary of State conceded incompatibility with Article 8 ECHR but opposed making a section 4 declaration while a comprehensive Mental Health Bill remained in consultation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim for a declaration of incompatibility under section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration of incompatibility granted; sections 26 and 29 of the 1983 Act were incompatible with Article 8 in failing to allow a patient to apply to replace an unsuitable nearest relative.
enrichment.ratio: Where a patient reasonably objects to her nearest relative and no effective means exists to replace him, the automatic nearest relative scheme produces a disproportionate interference with Article 8; admission of incompatibility does not remove the court's discretion to make a section 4 declaration when legislative reform remains uncertain.
legal_issues: Compatibility of nearest relative provisions with Article 8 ECHR
Whether a section 4 declaration is necessary where incompatibility is admitted
Discretion to decline a declaration pending comprehensive legislative reform
Effect of regulation 14 delegation by the nearest relative

confidence.notes: Incompatibility conceded; judgment focuses on section 4 discretion with clear outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Commodity resin formulations not confidential trade secrets
key_facts: Cray Valley sued Deltech and former Borden employees for misuse of alkyd and polyester resin formulations after Deltech acquired the Haverhill factory.
The formulations were standard commodity products, partly published in industry guides, unmarked as confidential and left on site when Cray departed.
Jacob J held no breach of confidence because the information lacked the necessary quality of confidence and no reasonable obligation bound the ex-Borden team.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Chancery Division on breach of confidence, copyright infringement and abandoned conspiracy and database right claims.
enrichment.outcome: Breach of confidence claim dismissed against all defendants; copyright infringement established but financial remedies left for further argument.
enrichment.ratio: Standard resin formulations widely known to skilled chemists, published in part and never protected by the former employer cannot be enforced as confidential against ex-employees where no duty of confidence was communicated and the information was of slight economic value in the defendants' hands.
legal_issues: Whether resin formulations had the necessary quality of confidence
Whether information was imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence
Industry practice and Coco v Clark tests for breach of confidence
Ownership and assignment of copyright in manufacturing documents
Availability of injunction where information is largely remembered

confidence.notes: Fact-heavy technical trial with clear conclusions on confidence and copyright chain of title.

enrichment.short_title: Combined mews properties as enfranchiseable house
key_facts: Mrs Collins held a head lease combining nos 11 and 12 Devonshire Mews South, linked by a communicating door and used largely as one residence with a separately let flat in no 12.
She claimed enfranchisement of the combined property; Howard de Walden argued they were two houses or vertically divided under section 2(1)(b).
The judge held the properties were one house reasonably so called; the Court of Appeal dismissed the freeholder's appeal after Malekshad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against a declaration that the tenant was entitled to acquire the freehold under the Leasehold Reform Act 1967.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; nos 11 and 12 together constituted a house for enfranchisement and were not vertically divided within section 2(1)(b).
enrichment.ratio: Under Malekshad, section 2(1)(b) excludes a vertically divided building only where the division separates distinct residential units; where an integral garage and utility room in one mews house are accessed through a party-wall door, the combined property may reasonably be called one house.
legal_issues: Whether adjoining mews properties are one house reasonably so called
Application of section 2(1)(b) vertical division test
Effect of a communicating door and separate flat on enfranchisement
Distinction from Malekshad on facts

linked_authorities.name: Malekshad v Howard de Walden Estates Ltd
Tandon v Trustees of Spurgeons Homes
Malpas v St Ermin's Property Ltd

confidence.notes: Post-House of Lords guidance applied to distinct facts; both structure and user issues addressed.

enrichment.short_title: Football club claim struck out for CPR default
key_facts: Bournemouth and Boscombe Athletic issued a claim against Lloyds TSB at the limitation deadline alleging breach of a 1994 loan facility and a tortious duty of care.
The club served the claim form on the last day but particulars of claim late, acting in person after briefly instructing solicitors, repeating conduct from an earlier struck-out action.
Peter Smith J refused an extension under CPR 3.9 and struck out the claim; the bank would in any event have had summary judgment on duty of care and insolvency-based default.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to strike out or obtain summary judgment and for extension of time to serve particulars of claim under the CPR.
enrichment.outcome: Extension refused and claim struck out; the club's deliberate procedural defaults and second identical action warranted no further indulgence.
enrichment.ratio: Repeated last-minute issue of generic claim forms, failure to serve particulars, and deliberate delay constitute intentional non-compliance with the CPR such that relief under rule 3.9 is refused, especially where the action repeats a previously struck-out claim and the defendant has a strong merits defence.
legal_issues: Extension of time to serve particulars after expiry under CPR 3.9
Strike out for failure to comply with CPR 7.4
Whether a bank owes a tortious duty of disclosure to its customer
Whether wrongful demand under a loan agreement had real prospect of success
Abuse of process in a second action repeating a struck-out claim

linked_authorities.name: Sabrina Robert v Momentum Services Ltd
Suriya and Douglas v Midland Bank Plc

confidence.notes: Procedural decision with full chronology; contract merits addressed obiter on Part 24 test.

enrichment.short_title: Harrier training noise nuisance at Walcot Hall
key_facts: Mr Dennis complained that Harrier jet training circuits from RAF Wittering caused extreme noise over his Grade I listed estate near Stamford.
The MOD conceded the aircraft were noisy and the noise reduced the property's market value, but argued national security justified continuing training.
Buckley J held a nuisance was established but refused an injunction; he awarded £950,000 damages reflecting blight, loss of amenity and lost commercial use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court claim for declaration and damages for private nuisance and Human Rights Act claims relating to aircraft noise.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration refused; damages of £950,000 awarded for nuisance; Human Rights Act claims satisfied by the common law award.
enrichment.ratio: Extreme military aircraft noise can constitute a private nuisance, but where training pilots is a compelling public interest the court may withhold injunctive relief and award compensation instead, treating public benefit as relevant at the remedy stage rather than denying a cause of action.
legal_issues: Whether Harrier training noise is a private nuisance
Public interest as a defence to nuisance or factor at remedy stage
Prescriptive rights to commit nuisance by 20 years' flying
Quantum of blight and loss of amenity damages
Article 8 and Article 1 Protocol 1 compatibility and just satisfaction

linked_authorities.name: Marcic v Thames Water Utilities Ltd

confidence.notes: Comprehensive trial judgment with detailed noise findings and nuanced public-interest analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Forfeiture rule upheld after manslaughter killing
key_facts: Dominic Dalton strangled his elderly partner B.M. after a row; he was convicted of manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility and sentenced to six years.
He was sole beneficiary under B.M.'s 1996 will but forfeited the estate under the public policy rule precluding killers from benefiting.
He applied under section 2 of the Forfeiture Act 1982 for relief, seeking to inherit the Brighton home and remaining estate of about £161,000.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application in the Chancery Division for an order modifying the forfeiture rule under section 2 of the Forfeiture Act 1982.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; justice did not require modifying the forfeiture rule given moral culpability and exploitation of the deceased.
enrichment.ratio: Manslaughter by diminished responsibility falls within the forfeiture rule and section 2 relief requires positive satisfaction that justice demands modification; significant moral culpability, financial exploitation and family objection may justify refusing relief even where responsibility for the killing was reduced.
legal_issues: Application of the forfeiture rule to manslaughter by diminished responsibility
Scope of discretion under section 2(2) of the Forfeiture Act 1982
Relevance of conduct towards the deceased before the killing
Whether mental illness alone warrants relief from forfeiture

confidence.notes: Detailed fact-finding on relationship and expenditure; clear refusal of section 2 relief.
